quote: I don’t know if the Sophisticate’s mistake has an official name, but I call it the Fallacy of Gray.
content: The continuum fallacy says that because there is no sharp line, the ends do not differ. The Fallacy of Gray says that because nothing is pure white, all grays are the same, and its main application here is to probabilities: "there's still a chance" as a license to ignore odds of 2<sup>−750,000,000</sup>. That use, uncertainty levelled into equivalence, is not the beard. "False equivalence" names the conclusion without naming the route to it. The essay's "I don't know if the Sophisticate's mistake has an official name" is an honest disclaimer, and its name has spread because it picks out the route, from "not perfect" to "no better." Fable's own summary is "Nothing here is wrong."

quote: many bloggers have said of Overcoming Bias: “It is impossible, no one can completely eliminate bias.”
content: The quoted objection is "It is impossible, no one can completely eliminate bias," which is about elimination, and the essay answers it. The stronger measurement objection has an answer too: you keep score. Calibration and forecasting accuracy are measurable in oneself. Proper scoring rules exist to measure them, and the forecasting tournaments showed that people who received training and kept score got measurably better (Mellers et al. 2014). The bias blind spot can itself be measured and varies reliably across individuals (Scopelliti et al. 2015), and in the training trials Fable cites it went down (Morewedge et al. 2015). You cannot introspect your way to a measurement, and the essay does not ask you to. It asks you to try to do better, and the score shows whether you have.

quote: then in many cases I don’t think it’s unreasonable to call the output “straightforward”—even in economics
content: Gordon and Dahl found that on most questions put to the IGM panel of elite economists there was no significant split between Democrat-leaning and Republican-leaning members, and substantial consensus (Gordon & Dahl 2013). That is "in many cases," which is all the essay claims. Fuchs, Krueger and Poterba found that values drive disagreement on policies where the parameters are uncertain, which is where filters would be expected to operate. The essay's claim is comparative, "you can try to minimize that effect, or you can do things that are bound to increase it," and the data show both an area of consensus where the filter is thin and a contested area where it is thick. That is shades of gray, measured, and it is Hanson's position, not Cowen's claim that "there is no other way it can be."

quote: It’s a most peculiar psychology—this business of “Science is based on faith too, so there!”
content: Farias et al. describe how laypeople hold their trust in science. The essay is about the epistemic status of the thing trusted: the Moon predicted "to twelve decimal places" against the dragon healing a daughter. Those are different degrees of uncertainty however the believer holds them. The pessimistic meta-induction is answered by the Asimov passage the essay ends with. Superseded theories were wrong by smaller and smaller amounts, and their successful structure was retained: Fresnel's equations survived the ether (Worrall 1989). The "devil's bargain" is also conditional. The essay distinguishes the critic who names "specific problems X, Y, and Z," whom it welcomes, from the one who says "it's gray!" without pointing to anything, and says only that it "begins to suspect" the second.

quote: Or even if not, we can still compare shades, and say “it is darker” or “it is lighter.”
content: For the essay's main application the axis is given: probability is a scalar, and "the Moon rises tomorrow" is lighter than "the dragon heals her" on it. For calibration there is a single proper metric. The log score combines calibration and discrimination into one number. For multidimensional moral cases, the Fallacy of Gray is refuted by any Pareto comparison. Gandhi against Stalin is easy because one dominates on nearly every dimension, and the Sophisticate's claim that "no one is better than anyone else" fails as soon as one such comparison exists. Hard incommensurable cases exist, but the Sophisticate's universal levelling needs every case to be incommensurable, and the essay needs only that some are not.
